claims.text: Tungsten particles will be pre-coated with a thin nickel interlayer by vapor deposition and then consolidated by spark plasma sintering.
A nickel interlayer improves wettability between tungsten and copper.
A nickel interlayer improves bonding between tungsten and copper.
Nickel pre-coating reduces void formation in SPS-processed W–Cu composites.
Nickel pre-coating reduces phase separation in SPS-processed W–Cu composites.
Nickel-coated W–Cu will be more uniform and durable than W–Cu made by conventional SPS or vapor coating without a nickel interlayer.
Conventionally consolidated W regions or particles in a Cu matrix typically exhibit interfacial defects, voids, and phase separation.
Spark plasma sintering can densify tungsten-based powder materials.
The nickel interlayer acts as a wetting promoter by reducing interfacial-energy differences.
Reduced interfacial-energy differences enhance copper infiltration and bonding to tungsten surfaces.
Lowering the interfacial-energy barrier with a nickel coating facilitates a transient liquid phase during sintering.
The proposed transient liquid phase enhances contact between tungsten and copper.
Enhanced W–Cu contact reduces voids and improves structural connectivity.
Improved structural connectivity produces better thermal transport and mechanical durability.
Nickel-coated samples will have a lower void fraction than otherwise identical uncoated SPS controls.
Nickel-coated samples will have more uniform W–Cu interfaces than uncoated SPS controls.
Nickel-coated samples will have higher thermal conductivity than uncoated SPS controls.
Nickel-coated samples will retain greater mechanical strength under simulated fusion-reactor conditions than uncoated SPS controls.
Conventional SPS and vapor-coated tungsten composites without nickel have been observed to suffer from incomplete contact and defect formation.
Potential irradiation-induced destabilization of the nickel phase bounds the proposed service regime.
